imc-1996-01.title: Column and row operations
imc-1996-01.body:
The matrix has size $(n+1)\times(n+1)$; index rows and columns by $0,\dots,n$, so $A_{ij}=a_{|i-j|}$.

**Step 1.** Add column $0$ to column $n$. The new entry in row $i$ is $a_i+a_{n-i}=2a_0+nd=a_0+a_n$, the same in every row. Factor it out:
$$\det A=(a_0+a_n)\det A',$$
where $A'$ is $A$ with last column replaced by all ones.

**Step 2.** For $i=n,n-1,\dots,1$ (in this order), subtract row $i-1$ from row $i$. For $j<i$ the new entry is $a_{i-j}-a_{i-1-j}=d$. For $j\ge i$ it is $a_{j-i}-a_{j-i+1}=-d$. In the last column it is $1-1=0$. Row $0$ stays $(a_0,a_1,\dots,a_{n-1},1)$.

**Step 3.** Expand along the last column. Its only non-zero entry is the $1$ in row $0$, with sign $(-1)^{0+n}$. The remaining $n\times n$ minor $C$ has entries $d$ on and below the diagonal and $-d$ above it:
$$\det A=(-1)^n(a_0+a_n)\det\begin{pmatrix}d&-d&\cdots&-d\\d&d&\cdots&-d\\ \vdots&&\ddots&\vdots\\d&d&\cdots&d\end{pmatrix}.$$

**Step 4.** Add the last row $(d,\dots,d)$ to each of the other rows. Row $r$ becomes $2d$ in columns $\le r$ and $0$ to the right of the diagonal. The matrix is now lower triangular with diagonal $2d,\dots,2d,d$ ($n-1$ entries $2d$). So $\det C=(2d)^{n-1}d=2^{n-1}d^n$ and
$$\det A=(-1)^n(a_0+a_n)\,2^{n-1}d^n .$$
Check with $n=1$: $\det\begin{pmatrix}a_0&a_0+d\\a_0+d&a_0\end{pmatrix}=-d(2a_0+d)$. ✓

**Answer: $\det A=(-1)^n(a_0+a_n)2^{n-1}d^n$.**

imc-1996-02.title: Fold the interval, then a recursion
imc-1996-02.body:
Call the integral $I_n$. The integrand is continuous on $[-\pi,\pi]$ once its removable singularities at $0,\pm\pi$ are filled in. In the part over $[-\pi,0]$ substitute $x\mapsto-x$; the quotient $\frac{\sin nx}{\sin x}$ is even, so
$$I_n=\int_0^\pi\frac{\sin nx}{\sin x}\Big(\frac1{1+2^x}+\frac1{1+2^{-x}}\Big)dx=\int_0^\pi\frac{\sin nx}{\sin x}\,dx,$$
because $\frac1{1+2^x}+\frac{2^x}{2^x+1}=1$. For $n\ge3$,
$$I_n-I_{n-2}=\int_0^\pi\frac{\sin nx-\sin(n-2)x}{\sin x}\,dx=\int_0^\pi2\cos\big((n-1)x\big)\,dx=0 .$$
Also $I_1=\int_0^\pi1\,dx=\pi$ and $I_2=\int_0^\pi2\cos x\,dx=0$. Hence $I_n=\pi$ for odd $n$ and $I_n=0$ for even $n$.

**Answer: $\pi$ if $n$ is odd, $0$ if $n$ is even.**

imc-1996-02.title: Dirichlet-kernel expansion
imc-1996-02.body:
After the same folding step, $I_n=\int_0^\pi\frac{\sin nx}{\sin x}dx$. Since
$$\frac{\sin nx}{\sin x}=\frac{e^{inx}-e^{-inx}}{e^{ix}-e^{-ix}}=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}e^{i(n-1-2j)x}=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\cos\big((n-1-2j)x\big)$$
(the last step pairs $j$ with $n-1-j$), and $\int_0^\pi\cos(mx)\,dx$ equals $\pi$ for $m=0$ and $0$ for every other integer $m$, $I_n$ equals $\pi$ times the number of $j\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ with $n-1=2j$. There is exactly one such $j$ if $n$ is odd, and none if $n$ is even.

**Answer: $\pi$ if $n$ is odd, $0$ if $n$ is even.**

imc-1996-03.title: Eigenspace decomposition and simultaneous diagonalization
imc-1996-03.body:
We work over $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ (any field in which $2\ne0$).

**(i)** Let $V_\pm=\{v:Av=\pm v\}$. For any $v$,
$$v=\underbrace{\tfrac12(v+Av)}_{\in V_+}+\underbrace{\tfrac12(v-Av)}_{\in V_-},$$
since $A(v\pm Av)=Av\pm A^2v=Av\pm v=\pm(v\pm Av)$. Also $V_+\cap V_-=0$, because $v=Av=-v$ forces $v=0$. So $V=V_+\oplus V_-$, and a basis of $V_+$ together with a basis of $V_-$ is a basis of $V$ consisting of eigenvectors of $A$.

**(ii)** *Claim:* any family $\mathcal F$ of pairwise commuting involutions has a common eigenbasis. We use induction on $n$; $n=1$ is trivial. If every member of $\mathcal F$ is $\pm E$, any basis works. Otherwise pick $A_1\in\mathcal F$ with $V_+,V_-$ both non-zero, hence both of dimension $<n$. For $B\in\mathcal F$ and $v\in V_\pm$: $A_1Bv=BA_1v=\pm Bv$, so $V_\pm$ is invariant under every $B\in\mathcal F$. The restrictions of the members of $\mathcal F$ to $V_+$ are commuting involutions of $V_+$, so by induction $V_+$ has a common eigenbasis, and likewise $V_-$. Their union is a common eigenbasis of $V$.

In such a basis every member of $\mathcal F$ is diagonal with entries in $\{1,-1\}$ (the only eigenvalues of an involution, since $\lambda^2=1$). Distinct operators give distinct diagonal sign vectors, and there are $2^n$ of those. So $|\mathcal F|\le2^n$.

The bound is attained: in a fixed basis, the $2^n$ matrices $\operatorname{diag}(\pm1,\dots,\pm1)$ are distinct, pairwise commuting involutions.

**Answer: (ii) $2^n$.** ∎

imc-1996-04.title: Two inductive geometric bounds
imc-1996-04.body:
All $a_n$ are positive. Separating the terms $k=1,n-1$ (each $a_1a_{n-1}=a_{n-1}$) and $k=2,n-2$ (each $a_2a_{n-2}=\frac12a_{n-2}$), we get for $n\ge5$
$$a_n=\frac2na_{n-1}+\frac1na_{n-2}+\frac1n\sum_{k=3}^{n-3}a_ka_{n-k}, \qquad (\ast)$$
and for $n\ge3$
$$a_n=\frac2na_{n-1}+\frac1n\sum_{k=2}^{n-2}a_ka_{n-k}.\qquad(\ast\ast)$$
First values: $a_2=\frac12$, $a_3=\frac13$, $a_4=\frac14\big(2\cdot\frac13+\frac14\big)=\frac{11}{48}$.

**(i)** Let $q=0.7$. We claim $a_n\le q^n$ for $n\ge3$. It holds for $n=3,4$: $\frac13<0.343$ and $\frac{11}{48}<0.2401$. Suppose it holds for $3\le m\le N-1$, where $N\ge5$. The sum in $(\ast)$ has $N-5$ terms, each with both indices $\ge3$, so each is at most $q^N$. Hence
$$a_N\le\frac2Nq^{N-1}+\frac1Nq^{N-2}+\frac{N-5}Nq^N=\frac{q^N}{N}\Big(\frac2q+\frac1{q^2}+N-5\Big)\le q^N,$$
because $\frac2q+\frac1{q^2}=2.857\ldots+2.040\ldots<5$. Therefore $\limsup a_n^{1/n}\le0.7<0.7071\ldots=2^{-1/2}$.

**(ii)** Let $q=\frac23$. We claim $a_n\ge q^n$ for $n\ge2$. It holds for $n=2$: $\frac12>\frac49$. Suppose it holds for $2\le m\le N-1$, where $N\ge3$. The sum in $(\ast\ast)$ has $N-3$ terms, each at least $q^N$. Hence
$$a_N\ge\frac2Nq^{N-1}+\frac{N-3}Nq^N=\frac{q^N}N\Big(\frac2q+N-3\Big)=q^N,$$
since $\frac2q=3$. Therefore $a_n^{1/n}\ge\frac23$ for all $n\ge2$, and $\limsup a_n^{1/n}\ge\frac23$. ∎

imc-1996-05.title: Squeeze with linear and exponential bounds
imc-1996-05.body:
Throughout, $J_n(g)=n\int g(x)^n\,dx$ over the relevant interval.

**(i), case $a<0$.** Write $p(x)=1+ax+bx^2\in[0,1]$ on $[0,1]$ (it is $\le1+ax\le1$).

*Upper bound:* $p(x)\le1+ax\le e^{ax}$, so
$$n\int_0^1p^n\le n\int_0^1e^{anx}dx=\frac{1-e^{an}}{|a|}\to\frac1{|a|}.$$
*Lower bound:* fix small $\eta\in(0,1)$ and put $c=|a|+|b|\eta$, with $\eta$ small enough that $c\eta<1$. For $x\in[0,\eta]$, $p(x)=1-|a|x-|b|x^2\ge1-cx\ge0$, so
$$n\int_0^1p^n\ge n\int_0^\eta(1-cx)^ndx=\frac{n}{c(n+1)}\Big(1-(1-c\eta)^{n+1}\Big)\to\frac1c .$$
So $\liminf\ge\frac1{|a|+|b|\eta}$ for every small $\eta$, i.e. $\liminf\ge\frac1{|a|}$. Hence the limit is $\frac1{|a|}=-\frac1a$.

**(i), case $a\ge0$.** For $x\ge0$, $p(x)\ge1+bx^2$. For $n+1>|b|$ and $0\le x\le\frac1{\sqrt{n+1}}\ (\le1)$ we get $p(x)\ge1+\frac b{n+1}>0$. Hence
$$n\int_0^1p^n\ge\frac{n}{\sqrt{n+1}}\Big(1+\frac b{n+1}\Big)^n\to\infty,$$
because $\big(1+\frac b{n+1}\big)^n\to e^b>0$.

The same proof works on any interval $[0,A]$, $A>0$, in place of $[0,1]$ (only $p\ge0$ on $[0,A]$ is needed). Call this (i$'$).

**(ii)** Let $M=\max f$. If $M<1$, then $J_n(f)\le nM^n\to0$. If $M>1$, then $f>1$ on an interval of length $\ell>0$, so $J_n(f)\ge n\ell\to\infty$. Both contradict $0<L<\infty$, so $M=1$. Let $m=\min_{[0,1]}f''\le0$.

*$f'$ does not vanish on $[0,1]$.* Suppose $f'(x_0)=0$. Since $f$ is concave, $x_0$ is a maximum point, so $f(x_0)=1$. If $x_0<1$, Taylor's formula gives $f(x_0+h)\ge1+\frac m2h^2$ for $0\le h\le1-x_0$. Choose $\delta\in(0,1-x_0]$ with $1+\frac m2\delta^2>0$. By (i$'$) with $a=0$,
$$J_n(f)\ge n\int_0^\delta\Big(1+\frac m2h^2\Big)^ndh\to\infty .$$
If $x_0=1$, argue the same way with $h\le0$. Either way this is a contradiction. So $f'$ has no zero, and by continuity it has constant sign.

*The value of $L$.* Say $f'<0$; the case $f'>0$ is symmetric under $x\mapsto1-x$. Then $f$ is strictly decreasing, so $f(0)=1$. Since $f''\le0$, $f'$ is decreasing, so $|f'|=-f'$ is increasing and $\min|f'|=|f'(0)|=:\kappa>0$. By Taylor's formula and concavity,
$$1-\kappa h+\tfrac m2h^2\le f(h)\le1-\kappa h\qquad(0\le h\le1).$$
Choose $A\in(0,1)$ with $1-\kappa A+\frac m2A^2>0$. By (i$'$), both $n\int_0^A(1-\kappa h)^ndh$ and $n\int_0^A\big(1-\kappa h+\frac m2h^2\big)^ndh$ tend to $\frac1\kappa$, so $n\int_0^Af^n\to\frac1\kappa$. Moreover $n\int_A^1f^n\le nf(A)^n\to0$, since $0\le f(A)<1$. Therefore
$$L=\frac1\kappa=\frac1{\min_{[0,1]}|f'|},\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad\min_{[0,1]}|f'|=L^{-1}.$$
∎

imc-1996-06.title: Covers, projections and a case analysis
imc-1996-06.body:
**(a)** Taking the single set $E_1=L$ gives $C(L)\le\operatorname{length}(L)=\ell$. Conversely, let $L\subset\bigcup_{i=1}^nE_i$ and identify $L$ with $[0,\ell]$. The set $F_i=E_i\cap L$ is contained in the closed interval $[\inf F_i,\sup F_i]$, whose length is $\operatorname{diam}F_i\le\operatorname{diam}E_i$ (empty $F_i$ are dropped). These intervals cover $[0,\ell]$, so by subadditivity of length (Lebesgue measure),
$$\ell\le\sum_i\operatorname{diam}F_i\le\sum_i\operatorname{diam}E_i .$$
Hence $C(L)=\ell$.

**(b)** Let $f$ be a contraction of $E$ onto a segment $L$, and $E\subset\bigcup E_i$. Then $L=f(E)\subset\bigcup f(E_i\cap E)$ and $\operatorname{diam}f(E_i\cap E)\le\operatorname{diam}E_i$. By (a), $\operatorname{length}(L)\le\sum\operatorname{diam}E_i$. Taking the infimum over covers and then the supremum over $L$ gives $K(E)\le C(E)$.

**(c)** Let $E=T\cup T'$ as in the hint. $E$ is compact.

We use repeatedly that the distance from a point to the points of a polygon (or of its convex hull) is maximized at a vertex.

*$C(E)=8$.* Comparing vertices, the largest distance between a point of $T$ and a point of $T'$ is $\operatorname{dist}((0,4),(0,-4))=8$; the other vertex pairs give at most $\sqrt{40}$. Within one triangle distances are at most $4$. So $\operatorname{diam}E=8$, and the cover $\{E\}$ gives $C(E)\le8$. For the lower bound, let $E\subset\bigcup_{i=1}^nE_i$, where we may assume every $E_i$ meets $E$.
- If no $E_i$ meets both $T$ and $T'$, the sets meeting $T$ cover the segment $[(-2,2),(2,2)]$, and the other sets cover $[(-2,-2),(2,-2)]$. By (a) each group has total diameter $\ge4$, so the sum is $\ge8$.
- If some $E_k$ contains points $a\in T$ and $b\in T'$, replace $E_k$ by $E_k\cup[a,b]$. This does not increase the diameter, because the distance from any point $z$ to a point of $[a,b]$ is at most $\max(|z-a|,|z-b|)$. The new family covers $T\cup[a,b]\cup T'$. Its orthogonal projection onto the $y$-axis contains $[2,4]$ (from $T$), $[-4,-2]$ (from $T'$) and $[-2,2]$ (from $[a,b]$, since $a_2\ge2$ and $b_2\le-2$), so it covers the segment $\{0\}\times[-4,4]$. Projection is a contraction, so by (b)'s argument and (a) the diameters add up to at least $8$.

So $C(E)=8$.

*$K(E)\le\sqrt{50}<8$.* Let $f$ contract $E$ onto $L=[a',b']$, and pick $a,b\in E$ with $f(a)=a'$, $f(b)=b'$. Then $\operatorname{length}(L)\le|a-b|$.
- If $a,b$ lie in the same triangle, $|a-b|\le\operatorname{diam}T=4$.
- So let $a\in T$, $b\in T'$. If $a_2\le3$, then $a$ lies in the convex hull of $(-2,2),(2,2),(-1,3),(1,3)$. The largest distance from these four points to the vertices $(\pm2,-2),(0,-4)$ of $T'$ is $\operatorname{dist}((\pm1,3),(0,-4))=\sqrt{50}$. So $|a-b|\le\sqrt{50}$. The case $b_2\ge-3$ is the same.
- Finally let $a_2>3$ and $b_2<-3$. Then $a$ lies in the triangle with vertices $(0,4),(\pm1,3)$, and every vertex of $T$ is within $\sqrt{10}$ of each of these three points (e.g. $\operatorname{dist}((1,3),(-2,2))=\sqrt{10}$). So every point of $T$ is within $\sqrt{10}$ of $a$, and hence $f(T)$ lies within $\sqrt{10}$ of the endpoint $a'$. Similarly $f(T')$ lies within $\sqrt{10}$ of $b'$. Since $f(T)\cup f(T')=L$, we get $\operatorname{length}(L)\le2\sqrt{10}<\sqrt{50}$.

So $K(E)\le\sqrt{50}<8=C(E)$, and equality in (b) fails for this compact set. ∎

imc-1996-07.title: Cluster points are fixed points
imc-1996-07.body:
*Only if:* if $x_n\to x$ then $x_{n+1}-x_n\to x-x=0$.

*If:* suppose $x_{n+1}-x_n\to0$ but $(x_n)$ does not converge. The sequence lies in $[0,1]$, so $K=\liminf x_n<L=\limsup x_n$.

**Step 1: every $c\in(K,L)$ is a cluster point.** Let $\varepsilon>0$ with $K<c-\varepsilon<c+\varepsilon<L$. For $n\ge n_0$ we have $|x_{n+1}-x_n|<2\varepsilon$. Infinitely many $x_n$ are $<c-\varepsilon$ and infinitely many are $>c+\varepsilon$. Each passage of the sequence (after $n_0$) from below $c-\varepsilon$ to above $c+\varepsilon$ uses steps shorter than $2\varepsilon$, so it cannot jump over the interval $(c-\varepsilon,c+\varepsilon)$ of length $2\varepsilon$. So infinitely many terms lie in $(c-\varepsilon,c+\varepsilon)$.

**Step 2: every $c\in(K,L)$ is a fixed point.** By Step 1, $x_{n_j}\to c$ for some subsequence. Then $x_{n_j+1}=f(x_{n_j})\to f(c)$ by continuity, and also $x_{n_j+1}=x_{n_j}+(x_{n_j+1}-x_{n_j})\to c$. So $f(c)=c$.

**Step 3: contradiction.** By Step 1 some term $x_N$ lies in $(K,L)$. By Step 2, $x_{N+1}=f(x_N)=x_N$, and inductively $x_n=x_N$ for all $n\ge N$. Then the sequence converges, contradicting $K<L$. ∎

imc-1996-08.title: Two quadratic relations, subtract
imc-1996-08.body:
**Lemma 1.** If $\cosh t\in\mathbb Q$, then $\cosh(jt)\in\mathbb Q$ for every $j\in\mathbb N$. This follows by induction from $\cosh0=1$ and
$$\cosh(j+1)t=2\cosh t\cosh jt-\cosh(j-1)t .$$

**Lemma 2.** Let $m\ge1$, $a=\cosh m\theta$, $b=\cosh(m+1)\theta$ and $c=\cosh\theta$. Then
$$c^2-2ab\,c+(a^2+b^2-1)=0 .$$
*Proof.* Since $\theta>0$, the sinh values are positive: $\sinh m\theta=\sqrt{a^2-1}$ and $\sinh(m+1)\theta=\sqrt{b^2-1}$. So
$$c=\cosh\big((m+1)\theta-m\theta\big)=ab-\sqrt{a^2-1}\sqrt{b^2-1}.$$
Hence $(ab-c)^2=(a^2-1)(b^2-1)$, which expands to the stated identity. $\square$

The claim is trivial for $k=1$, so let $k\ge2$. Put $a=\cosh k\theta$, $b=\cosh(k+1)\theta$ (rational by hypothesis), and
$$A=\cosh(k^2-1)\theta=\cosh\big((k-1)\cdot(k+1)\theta\big),\qquad B=\cosh k^2\theta=\cosh\big(k\cdot k\theta\big).$$
These are rational by Lemma 1. Since $k^2-1$ and $k^2$ are consecutive, Lemma 2 applies to both pairs:
$$c^2-2ab\,c+(a^2+b^2-1)=0,\qquad c^2-2AB\,c+(A^2+B^2-1)=0 .$$
Subtracting,
$$2(AB-ab)\,c=(A^2+B^2)-(a^2+b^2).$$
Since $k\ge2$ we have $k^2-1>k$, and $\cosh$ is increasing on $[0,\infty)$, so $A>a\ge1$ and $B>b\ge1$. Hence $AB>ab$, and
$$\cosh\theta=c=\frac{A^2+B^2-a^2-b^2}{2(AB-ab)}\in\mathbb Q .$$
∎

imc-1996-09.title: Identify $H$ with the dyadic rationals
imc-1996-09.body:
Let $M(x)=\begin{pmatrix}1&x\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbb D=\mathbb Z[\frac12]=\{p/2^s:p\in\mathbb Z,\ s\ge0\}$, the dyadic rationals.

**Shape of $G$.** The set $\Gamma=\Big\{\begin{pmatrix}2^m&x\\0&1\end{pmatrix}:m\in\mathbb Z,\ x\in\mathbb D\Big\}$ contains $A$ and $B$. It is closed under products, since $\begin{pmatrix}2^m&x\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}2^{m'}&x'\\0&1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2^{m+m'}&2^mx'+x\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$. It is closed under inverses, since $\begin{pmatrix}2^m&x\\0&1\end{pmatrix}^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}2^{-m}&-2^{-m}x\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$. Hence $G\subseteq\Gamma$, and every element of $H$ is $M(x)$ for some $x\in\mathbb D$.

**(a)** $M(x)M(y)=M(x+y)=M(y)M(x)$ and $M(x)^{-1}=M(-x)$. So $H$ contains the identity $M(0)$ and is closed under products and inverses: it is a subgroup of $G$, and it is abelian.

**(b)** For every $n\ge0$,
$$A^{-n}BA^n=\begin{pmatrix}2^{-n}&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}2^n&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1&2^{-n}\\0&1\end{pmatrix}=M(2^{-n})\in H.$$
Suppose $H$ were generated by finitely many elements $M(x_1),\dots,M(x_r)$ with $x_i=p_i/2^{s_i}$, and let $s=\max s_i$. Every product of these generators and their inverses is $M(x)$ with $x$ an integer combination of the $x_i$, so $x\in2^{-s}\mathbb Z$. But $M(2^{-s-1})\in H$ and $2^{-s-1}\notin2^{-s}\mathbb Z$. This contradiction shows that $H$ is not finitely generated. (In fact $H=\{M(x):x\in\mathbb D\}\cong(\mathbb D,+)$.) ∎

imc-1996-10.title: Inflate the disc along the free arc
imc-1996-10.body:
Arcs are taken closed. (For the square $[-1,1]^2$, whose maximal inscribed ellipse is the unit disc, $\Gamma\cap C$ consists of $4$ points spaced $\frac\pi2$ apart, so an *open* arc of length $\frac\pi2$ can miss $\Gamma$.) An arc of length $\ge\frac\pi2$ contains a closed arc of length exactly $\frac\pi2$, so it suffices to treat that case.

Suppose a closed arc $A\subset C$ of length $\frac\pi2$ misses $\Gamma$. After a rotation, $A$ is the arc from $N=(\frac1{\sqrt2},-\frac1{\sqrt2})$ to $M=(\frac1{\sqrt2},\frac1{\sqrt2})$ through $(1,0)$. Since $D\subset B$ and $B$ is closed, $A\subset B\setminus\Gamma=\operatorname{int}B$. By symmetry, $-A\subset\operatorname{int}B$ too. The set $A\cup(-A)$ is compact, so there is $\delta>0$ such that every point within distance $\delta$ of $A\cup(-A)$ lies in $B$.

For $0<\varepsilon<\delta$ let $u=(1+\varepsilon)^2>1$ and let $E_\varepsilon$ be the ellipse $\frac{x^2}{u}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}\le1$, with $b$ chosen so that $M$ lies on its boundary: $\frac1u+\frac1{b^2}=2$, i.e. $b^2=\frac{u}{2u-1}<1$. Its area is
$$\pi\sqrt u\,b=\pi\frac{u}{\sqrt{2u-1}}>\pi,$$
because $u^2>2u-1\iff(u-1)^2>0$. We show $E_\varepsilon\subset B$, which contradicts the maximality of $D$.

Let $(x,y)\in E_\varepsilon$. Using $\frac1{b^2}=2-\frac1u$,
$$x^2+y^2=\Big(\frac{x^2}u+\frac{y^2}{b^2}\Big)+\Big(1-\frac1u\Big)(x^2-y^2)\le1+\Big(1-\frac1u\Big)(x^2-y^2).$$
- If $|y|\ge|x|$, then $x^2+y^2\le1$, so $(x,y)\in D\subset B$.
- If $|x|>|y|$: the semi-axes of $E_\varepsilon$ are $1+\varepsilon$ and $b<1$, so $r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\le1+\varepsilon$. If $r\le1$ the point is in $D\subset B$. If $1<r\le1+\varepsilon$, the point $(x,y)/r$ lies on $C$ at an angle within $\frac\pi4$ of the $x$-axis, i.e. in $A\cup(-A)$, and its distance to $(x,y)$ is $r-1\le\varepsilon<\delta$. So $(x,y)\in B$.

Thus $E_\varepsilon\subset B$ and $\operatorname{area}E_\varepsilon>\pi=\operatorname{area}D$, which contradicts the assumption that $D$ is the ellipse of maximal area in $B$. Hence every closed arc of $C$ of length $\ge\frac\pi2$ meets $\Gamma$. ∎

*Remark.* The maximal-area ellipse inside a convex body is known as John's ellipse.

imc-1996-11.title: Midpoint rule with an explicit error term
imc-1996-11.body:
Let $f(t)=\dfrac{t}{(1+t^2)^2}$ and $h=x^{-1/2}\in(0,1]$. Then
$$h\,f(nh)=\frac{n h^2}{(1+n^2h^2)^2}=\frac{n/x}{(1+n^2/x)^2}=\frac{nx}{(n^2+x)^2},$$
so the sum equals $S(h)=h\sum_{n\ge1}f(nh)$. Also $\int_0^\infty f=\big[-\tfrac1{2(1+t^2)}\big]_0^\infty=\tfrac12$. It suffices to prove (ii), since it implies (i).

**Midpoint error.** For $g\in C^2[a-\beta,a+\beta]$, Taylor's formula with integral remainder, applied to $\int_0^\beta g(a\pm t)\,dt$, gives
$$\int_{a-\beta}^{a+\beta}g=2\beta g(a)+\frac12\int_0^\beta(\beta-t)^2\big(g''(a+t)+g''(a-t)\big)dt,$$
so
$$\Big|2\beta g(a)-\int_{a-\beta}^{a+\beta}g\Big|\le\frac{\beta^2}2\int_{a-\beta}^{a+\beta}|g''| .$$

**Estimate.** Let $J_n=[(n-\frac12)h,(n+\frac12)h]$. These intervals tile $[\frac h2,\infty)$, so
$$S(h)-\frac12=\sum_{n\ge1}\Big(hf(nh)-\int_{J_n}f\Big)-\int_0^{h/2}f .$$
Apply the midpoint estimate with $\beta=h/2$ to each term:
$$\Big|S(h)-\frac12\Big|\le\frac{h^2}8\int_{h/2}^\infty|f''|+\int_0^{h/2}t\,dt\le\frac{h^2}8\int_0^\infty|f''|+\frac{h^2}8 .$$
Here $f'(t)=\dfrac{1-3t^2}{(1+t^2)^3}$ and $f''(t)=\dfrac{12t(t^2-1)}{(1+t^2)^4}$. So $f''$ changes sign only at $t=1$, and
$$\int_0^\infty|f''|=|f'(1)-f'(0)|+|f'(\infty)-f'(1)|=\tfrac54+\tfrac14=\tfrac32 .$$
Therefore
$$\Big|\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{nx}{(n^2+x)^2}-\frac12\Big|\le\Big(\frac3{16}+\frac18\Big)h^2=\frac{5}{16}\cdot\frac1x\qquad(x\ge1),$$
which proves (ii) with $c=\frac5{16}$. Letting $x\to\infty$ proves (i). (Numerically, the error is about $-\frac1{12x}$.) ∎

imc-1996-12.title: AM-GM with optimal weights; near-extremal sequence
imc-1996-12.body:
**(i)** Let $c_n=\dfrac{(n+1)^n}{n^{n-1}}$. The product telescopes: $c_1c_2\cdots c_n=(n+1)^n$. By AM-GM,
$$(a_1\cdots a_n)^{1/n}=\frac{(a_1c_1\cdots a_nc_n)^{1/n}}{n+1}\le\frac{a_1c_1+\dots+a_nc_n}{n(n+1)} .$$
Sum over $n$ and exchange the order (all terms are positive):
$$\sum_{n\ge1}(a_1\cdots a_n)^{1/n}\le\sum_{k\ge1}a_kc_k\sum_{n\ge k}\frac1{n(n+1)}=\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{a_kc_k}{k}=\sum_{k\ge1}a_k\Big(1+\frac1k\Big)^k,$$
using $\sum_{n\ge k}\big(\frac1n-\frac1{n+1}\big)=\frac1k$. Since $(1+\frac1k)^k<e$ and $a_k>0$ for every $k$, and $\sum a_k<\infty$, the last sum is strictly less than $e\sum a_k$.

**(ii)** We may assume $0<\varepsilon<e$. Choose $K$ with $(1+\frac1n)^n>e-\frac\varepsilon2$ for $n>K$. For $N>K$ (to be chosen) let
$$a_n=\frac{n^{n-1}}{(n+1)^n}=\frac{1}{n(1+\frac1n)^n}\quad(n\le N),\qquad a_n=2^{-n}\quad(n>N).$$
The product telescopes again: $a_1\cdots a_n=\frac{1}{(n+1)^n}$, so $(a_1\cdots a_n)^{1/n}=\frac1{n+1}$ for $n\le N$. Let $H=\sum_{n=K+1}^N\frac1n$ and $C=\sum_{n\le K}a_n+1$, which does not depend on $N$. Then
$$\sum_n a_n\le C+\sum_{n=K+1}^N\frac{1}{n(1+\frac1n)^n}<C+\frac{H}{e-\varepsilon/2},\qquad \sum_n(a_1\cdots a_n)^{1/n}\ge\sum_{n=K+1}^N\frac1{n+1}\ge H-1 .$$
So it suffices that $H-1\ge(e-\varepsilon)\big(C+\frac H{e-\varepsilon/2}\big)$, i.e.
$$H\cdot\frac{\varepsilon/2}{e-\varepsilon/2}\ge1+(e-\varepsilon)C .$$
The left side tends to $\infty$ as $N\to\infty$ (harmonic series), so a suitable $N$ exists. For it, $\sum(a_1\cdots a_n)^{1/n}>(e-\varepsilon)\sum a_n$, with all $a_n>0$ and $\sum a_n<\infty$. So the constant $e$ in (i) is best possible. ∎
